title: Resilient Inference — Trust Messaging & Fallback Playbook
content:
Objective:
- Produce crisp go-to-market language and sales-ready anecdotes that explain how Redwood minimizes downtime and customer-visible regressions through layered fallbacks, multi-region routing, and predictable degraded modes.

Primary audience:
- Product and platform buyers evaluating inference providers (platform teams, infra leads)
- Developer leads concerned with reliability SLAs
- Customer success and sales reps who need concise incident narratives

Key single-line positioning:
- "Redwood keeps your LLM features alive: predictable fallbacks, fast regional failover, and transparent degradation policies so your product stays usable even during infra events."

Three core messages (short bullets for hero website and one-pager):
1) Predictable graceful degradation — degrade to a lower-cost/compatible model variant with bounded latency and preserved semantics rather than hard errors.
2) Multi-region failover & routing — policy-driven routing with warm replicas across regions so requests failover in <500ms for session continuity.
3) Observable trust — token-level traces, rollbackable rollouts, and transparent incident narratives so customers can audit impact and restore confidence.

Supporting proof points (engineer-friendly):
- Auto-fallback chains: primary model -> quantized variant -> response-cached stub -> structured error with user-friendly fallback text; each stage has SLOs and circuit-breaker thresholds.
- Warm prefix/KV caches replicated across regions to reduce cold-start impact during failovers.
- Smart routing: requests routed by latency and cost policy; can pin to region or tier for isolation; automated downgrade to dedicated capacity if supported.
- Measured outcomes: median tail p99 latency increase <20% during region failover in our benchmark, successful failovers in internal chaos tests 98% of attempts.

Incident narratives (sales-ready, human tone):
- Example A — Region outage, retail customer: a primary cloud region went down; Redwood detected elevated error rates, automatically rerouted 96% of traffic to warm replicas in 2nd region, degraded long-context summarization to a trimmed-mode for 7 minutes to preserve throughput, and restored full fidelity after 12 minutes. Customer-facing impact: transiently shortened summaries, no user-facing errors, 0 data exposure. Post-incident: full timeline, root cause, and mitigation delivered with token-level traces.
- Example B — Heavy load + model OOM: a sudden batch of inference jobs triggered OOM on a family of GPUs. Redwood’s serving runtime circuit-breaker gated the batch, spilled lower-priority requests to a quantized variant and served cached responses for repeated prompts. Recovery plan included automated autoscaling and a controlled rollback to prior model version. Customer impact: ~4% of requests saw shorter outputs; overall service stayed up.

Competitive differentiation notes:
- Against general cloud ML endpoints: Redwood provides intent-preserving fallbacks and structured degraded modes whereas general endpoints often return errors or significantly different outputs.
- Against LLM-API providers: competitors may have multi-region endpoints but lack integrated KV-prefix cache replication; their failover can mean cold-start tails. We market warm caches and preserved session continuity.
- Against self-hosted runtimes: customers might build fallbacks themselves, but that’s expensive and inconsistent. Redwood sells a consistent API + policy layer and operational SLAs.

Objections & rebuttals (sales enablement):
- "We can just retry on our side." -> Retries amplify load and can worsen outages; Redwood’s routing and circuit-breakers avoid retry storms and provide bounded degradation.
- "Fallbacks will change model outputs and break UX." -> Fallback chain is designed to maintain intent and structured outputs; we surface differences in a controlled way and offer preflight sim tests for customers.

Suggested trust language (short snippets):
- "Fail-safe inference: controlled degradation, not silent failures."
- "Warm failover across regions with auditable timelines."
- "Fallbacks that preserve intent — and your user experience."

Metrics to highlight in collateral (technical appendix):
- Typical failover time to warm replica: 200–500ms
- P99 latency uplift during failover: <25%
- Chaose test pass rate (failover + degraded-mode preservation): 97–99%
- SLA options: 99.9% (hosted) with dedicated capacity upgrade to 99.95% under contract

Assets to produce (next 6 weeks):
- Two-page sales brief + one-pager "How Redwood keeps your LLM features online" (for AE use).
- Incident timeline template and customer-facing postmortem copykit.
- Short video (60–90s) demo showing multi-region failover and fallback chain behavior.
- FAQ for security & compliance regarding failover and data residency.

Open questions / decisions:
- Should we publish numeric failover benchmarks publicly or keep them in gated docs? (ops/legal input needed)
- Level of technical detail for marketing site vs AE playbook — prefer layered approach: headline + expandable appendix.

Next steps / owners:
- Product marketing: draft one-pager (owner: Maya Chen) — due 2026-02-28.
- Eng: compile benchmark artifacts and run an expanded chaos matrix for public claim (owner: Omar Patel) — due 2026-03-07.
- Legal/Compliance: signoff on public metrics and language (owner: Elena García) — due 2026-03-12.

Notes to self / scribbles:
- keep messaging developer-first: include examples of request routing config (policy-as-code) in appendix.
- prioritize customer narratives with measurable time/impact stats rather than vague "high availability" claims.
